analysis.one_liner: Barred the EPA from setting any limit on total carbon dioxide emissions.
analysis.headline: A three-sponsor bill to stop the EPA from capping total carbon emissions from any state or source category was referred to a House subcommittee on December 18, 2015, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the Clean Air Act to forbid the EPA from setting, carrying out, or enforcing any cap on the combined carbon dioxide emissions of a state or of any category of polluters within a state [S3]. In practice, that would have blocked nationwide programs like the Clean Power Plan, which set state-by-state carbon limits for power plants [S2]. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power subcommittee, where it died without a hearing or vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Fossil-fuel-burning power plants and other large carbon emitters would gain the most: the bill would remove the legal basis for aggregate carbon caps, freeing them from state-level or industry-wide emission limits and the cost of cutting their carbon output [S3]. Utilities and coal producers facing rules like the Clean Power Plan would avoid compliance costs [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill flatly prohibits the EPA from establishing, implementing, or enforcing any limit on the aggregate carbon dioxide emissions of a state, or of any category or subcategory of sources within a state, overriding any provision of the Clean Air Act [S3].

Because most real-world carbon rules cap emissions at the state or industry level rather than at each individual smokestack, this wording would have blocked the main type of power-plant carbon regulation, such as state-by-state limits under the Clean Power Plan [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost of unchecked carbon emissions — greater air pollution, heat waves, storms, and other climate damages — along with the loss of a regulatory tool that EPA had used to reduce power-plant emissions [S2]. States and residents would also lose the ability to have their state's total emissions capped.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through pollution and climate costs

drawbacks.text: The bill would strip the EPA of its authority to limit total carbon emissions, removing the main policy tool used to cut power-plant pollution at the state and industry level [S3].
Blocking aggregate limits would push more of the cost of carbon pollution onto the public in the form of air quality and climate damages, rather than onto the emitters themselves [S2].
The blanket prohibition would also remove flexible options that states and industries sometimes prefer, such as emissions trading under a cap, by banning caps outright instead of tailoring them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits would go almost entirely to a small set of large carbon emitters in the form of avoided compliance costs, while the costs — added pollution and climate risk — would be spread across the whole public. The bill offers no offsetting protections or compensation, so its costs plainly outweigh its benefits for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power subcommittee three days after introduction, and it sat there until the Congress ended, with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Sensenbrenner introduced the bill on December 15, 2015, joined by Reps. Ribble and Grothman, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
On December 18, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, where it remained with no further action through the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017 [S5].
The bill drew only two cosponsors, and no committee or floor vote ever occurred [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Supporters of EPA carbon regulation came out ahead: the bill died in subcommittee, so the EPA's existing authority to set aggregate carbon limits was never taken away. The three sponsors and the emitters they sought to shield gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Anyone counting on EPA carbon limits

for.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit EPA aggregate carbon dioxide limits

for.name: Reps. Reid Ribble and Glenn Grothman
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction of the bill on December 15, 2015

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Power Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans from Wisconsin, and the bill's only two cosponsors were also Republicans; no Democrat supported it, though the bill never advanced far enough for a recorded vote [S4].

industries.industry: Fossil-fuel power plants and coal producers
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated the legal basis for state-level and industry-wide carbon caps, sparing these emitters the cost of cutting carbon dioxide output under rules like the Clean Power Plan. Their gain would come at the public's expense in pollution and climate damages [S2].

Without any aggregate carbon limits, there would be far less demand for wind, solar, and pollution-control investments that carbon rules drive. These industries' interest in the bill ran alongside the public's.
